title: Why Grading Teacher Performance Kills Growth
author: Dr Emanuele
summary: Emanuele opens with a first-person account of trainee teaching where every single lesson was graded on a four-point scale rather than every two or three weeks, creating a year of feeling judged and never good enough. The piece uses this as entry to a larger argument: grading individual lessons is not a neutral measurement tool but a practice that shifts teacher development from growth to judgment. The intellectual core exposes three problems: Outstanding is incoherent (any lesson has room for improvement on clearer explanation, more precise checks, better wait time); a 60-minute snapshot reduces a long-running instructional relationship to a single word with no context about planning or mastery; and attaching a grade or judgmental label at the end of supportive feedback resets the conversation from coaching to verdict. The practical recommendation is clean: stop assigning overall lesson grades, stop assigning grades to sub-categories within feedback, focus solely on specific actionable feedback about what was observed, why it was effective, and one or two high-leverage actions the teacher can practise next.
points: Grading individual lessons is not a neutral measurement tool; it shifts teacher development from growth-focused coaching to judgment-focused evaluation.
Any lesson can be marked Outstanding yet still have room for improvement, making the grade incoherent; a 60-minute snapshot reduces complex instructional work to a single word.
Attaching a grade or judgmental label at the end of feedback resets the conversation from coaching to verdict; removing the grade is a precondition for coaching that genuinely improves practice.
quotes: When I started my teacher training over ten years ago, I faced a series of challenges like the relentless planning burden and subpar mentoring among them. But there was another element that amplified my anxiety to levels I haven’t fully recovered from: the lesson grading system.

A 60-minute snapshot of a teacher managing a highly complex concept with a challenging class is reduced to a single word. This grade carries zero context about the teacher’s long-term planning, their mastery of instructional atoms, or their relationships with the students.
When you grade, you ruin the positivity of the process and shift the focus from growth to judgment.
In too many schools, a mentor provides excellent, supportive, constructive feedback, but then ruins the entire process by adding a grade or a judgmental label.
It doesn’t matter if you stop using numbers and switch to kinder, less judgmental words. The act of assigning a label remains a negative judgment that breeds anxiety and defensiveness.

This transforms the observation from a performance review into a coaching session, making the process one of collaboration and development rather than anxiety and judgment.” Archived from Dr Emanuele on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
